We're going to start out with just getting a feel for how the we
measure things in astrophysics.  The scales we need to consider are so
vast: from the subatomic to the size of the observable universe.  The
combination of units that we use in astrophysics is a bit of a matter
of culture.  We generally use cgs (centimeter-gram-second) system.[Cgs
is the One True System of Units.  Look at Maxwell's Equations in cgs
and then in SI (mks), and you'll see for yourself!]{.aside
.content-visible when-format="html"} But we also use
$\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$ for velocities, solar masses ($M_{\odot}$) for
masses, and astronomical units (AU) or parsecs (pc) for distance.  See
the formulae and constants sheet to get a handle on it.  We are going
to start off by getting a sense of scale, first with time, and then
with distance.


## Ages are long

Let's get an appreciation for the longest timespan that exists in
nature: the age of the Universe.  The age of the Universe is
13,700,000,000 years. We should write that as $1.37 \times
10^{10}\,\mathrm{yr}$, but we frequently have to use the most
convenient units. In this case, the age of the Universe is 13.7
billion years, or $13.7\,\mathrm{Gyr}$.

* Duration of this class ($1\,\mathrm{hr} \sim 1/10^4\,\mathrm{yr} = 10^{-4}\,\mathrm{yr}$)
* Football season ($0.4\,\mathrm{yr}$)
* Life of a human ($10^2\,\mathrm{yr}$)
* Oldest currently existing *species* of animal ($600\,\mathrm{Myr}$, a type of sponge)
* Age of Earth and Sun ($4.5\,\mathrm{Gyr}$)
* Age of the oldest galaxies ($13\,\mathrm{Gyr}$)

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}

### Exercises {#sec-exercises-ages}

1. Convert every entry in the list above to units of seconds.

   ::: {.callout-tip .help-hint collapse="true" title="Hint"}
   Everything here is already in years (or a multiple of years), so you only
   need one conversion factor: the number of seconds in a year.

   $$
   1\,\mathrm{yr} = 365.25\,\mathrm{d} \times 24\,\frac{\mathrm{hr}}{\mathrm{d}}
   \times 3600\,\frac{\mathrm{s}}{\mathrm{hr}} = 3.156 \times 10^{7}\,\mathrm{s}
   $$

   Worth committing to memory, because of a coincidence that is genuinely
   useful: $\pi \times 10^{7}\,\mathrm{s}$ is within half a percent of a year.
   If you can remember $\pi$, you can remember the length of a year.
   :::

   ::: {.callout-note .help-answer collapse="true" title="Answers"}
   * Duration of this class: $3.16 \times 10^{3}\,\mathrm{s}$
     (exactly $3600\,\mathrm{s}$, since one hour is a little over
     $10^{-4}\,\mathrm{yr}$)
   * Football season: $1.26 \times 10^{7}\,\mathrm{s}$
   * Life of a human: $3.16 \times 10^{9}\,\mathrm{s}$
   * Oldest currently existing species of animal: $1.89 \times 10^{16}\,\mathrm{s}$
   * Age of Earth and Sun: $1.42 \times 10^{17}\,\mathrm{s}$
   * Age of the oldest galaxies: $4.10 \times 10^{17}\,\mathrm{s}$
   :::

:::

## Sizes are big

Douglas Adams once wrote "Space is big. You just won't believe how
vastly, hugely, mind-bogglingly big it is. I mean, you may think it's
a long way down the road to the chemist's, but that's just peanuts to
space" [@adams1979].  So let's try to wrap our head around these mind-bogglingly
big numbers.


* Size of Ann Arbor ($10\,\mathrm{km} = 10^{-12}\,\mathrm{ly}$)
* Circumference of Earth ($40{,}000\,\mathrm{km} = 4 \times 10^{-9}\,\mathrm{ly}$)
* Distance to Moon ($400{,}000\,\mathrm{km} = 4 \times 10^{-8}\,\mathrm{ly}$)
* Distance to Sun (150 million km $= 1.6 \times 10^{-5}\,\mathrm{ly}$)
* The Nearest Star (40 trillion km $= 4.5\,\mathrm{ly}$)
* Diameter of our Milky Way Galaxy (100,000 light years)
* Size of Observable Universe (10 billion light years)

:::: {.callout-note .worked-example title="Worked example: the size of the Universe in km"}
Given the speed of light, what is the size of the Universe in km?

The two numbers we need are the speed of light,

$$
c \equiv \mathrm{speed\ of\ light} = 2.9979246 \times 10^{10}\,\mathrm{cm\,s^{-1}}
$$ {#eq-c}

and the distance light covers in a year,

$$
1\,\mathrm{light\ year} = 9.46 \times 10^{12}\,\mathrm{km}
$$ {#eq-lightyear}

A light year is a *distance*, not a time — it is how far light gets in one year,
which is why @eq-c and @eq-lightyear are two ways of saying the same thing. So
the conversion is a single multiplication, and we take the size of the
observable Universe from the list above as $10^{10}\,\mathrm{ly}$.

**Write the known equivalence as a fraction, and keep the units attached.**
The equivalence in @eq-lightyear can be made into a fraction two ways up, and
**you choose by asking which arrangement cancels the unit you are trying to get
rid of.** Here the light years have to go, so they belong in the denominator:

$$
10^{10}\,\mathrm{ly} \times
\frac{9.46 \times 10^{12}\,\mathrm{km}}{1\,\mathrm{ly}}
$$

**Now cancel the units, still without touching the numbers.** There is one
factor of $\mathrm{ly}$ on the top and one on the bottom, and they cancel,
leaving $\mathrm{km}$. *Do the units make sense?* Kilometers are a length, and
the size of the Universe is a length, so yes.

**This is why the fraction is worth writing out rather than just multiplying by
$9.46 \times 10^{12}$.** Had you put it the other way up, as
$1\,\mathrm{ly} / 9.46 \times 10^{12}\,\mathrm{km}$, nothing would have
canceled and you would have been left with $\mathrm{ly^{2}\,km^{-1}}$ — which is
not a length. The setup tells you whether to multiply or divide, so you never
have to remember which. Every conversion from here on is written out this way.

**Only now, the numbers.**

$$
10^{10} \times 9.46 \times 10^{12}\,\mathrm{km} = 9.46 \times 10^{22}\,\mathrm{km}
$$

Which is a number so large that writing it in kilometers has done nothing
whatsoever to help you picture it. That is the point of light years.
::::


I've used lightyears above, but that's only because you've heard of
them before.  A legit astrophysicist would only use parsec.  For
reference, $1\,\mathrm{pc} \approx 3.26\,\mathrm{lyr} \approx 3.09
\times 10^{18}\,\mathrm{cm}$.



::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}

   ::: {.callout-note .help-answer collapse="true" title="Answers"}

   * Circumference of Earth: $1.2 \times 10^{-9}\,\mathrm{pc}$
   * Distance to Moon: $1.2 \times 10^{-8}\,\mathrm{pc}$
   * Distance to Sun: $4.9 \times 10^{-6}\,\mathrm{pc}$
   * The Nearest Star: $1.4\,\mathrm{pc}$
   * Diameter of our Milky Way Galaxy: $3.1 \times 10^{4}\,\mathrm{pc} = 31\,\mathrm{kpc}$
   * Size of Observable Universe: $3.1 \times 10^{9}\,\mathrm{pc} = 3.1\,\mathrm{Gpc}$
   :::

:::


## Time "travel"


The speed of light is finite. As we said in @eq-c, it is $2.9979246
\times 10^{10}\,\mathrm{cm\,s^{-1}}$. Because of this, it takes time
for light to get to us, and we are seeing things as they were some
time ago.  So all of those distances above indicate how long ago we
are seeing them.



## Escape velocity

As we will see, black holes prevent light from escaping. In a (slightly
incorrect) Newtonian sense, we can think of black holes as objects that have
escape velocity greater than the speed of light, the ultimate speed limit.

You can derive escape velocity by setting the total energy (kinetic energy plus
gravitational potential energy) and setting it to zero:

$$
E_{\mathrm{tot}} = \frac{1}{2} m v^2 - \frac{G M m}{r} = 0,
$$ {#eq-energy}

where $m$ is the mass of the thing trying to escape (doesn't matter as long as
it is much less than the planet/black hole/whatever it is trying to escape
from), $M$ is the mass of the planet/black hole/whatever, $r$ is the radius at
which you have velocity $v$. The smallest $r$ can be for a planet is the radius
of the planet. $G = 6.67430 \times 10^{-8}\,\mathrm{cm^{3}\,g^{-1}\,s^{-2}}$ is
the gravitational constant. This is easy to solve:

$$
v_{\mathrm{esc}} = \left(\frac{2 G M}{r}\right)^{1/2}
$$ {#eq-vesc}

::: {.callout-tip .resolution collapse="true" title="Note the
dependencies on $M$ and $r$ and why."}
The *larger* the mass, the *higher* the
escape velocity.  Because bigger mass means stronger gravity, and
therefore harder to escape.  And the *smaller* the radius, the
*higher* the escape velocity because you are closer to the object,
which is where gravity is the strongest.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}

### Exercises {#sec-exercises-escape}

1. For the Earth ($M_{\oplus} = 5.97 \times 10^{27}\ \mathrm{g}$;
   $r_{\oplus} = 6.37 \times 10^{8}\ \mathrm{cm}$), what is the escape speed?

   ::: {.callout-note .help-solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
   **Substitute into @eq-vesc, and keep the units attached.** Escaping *from the
   surface* means the smallest $r$ can be, which is the radius of the Earth
   itself. Do not multiply anything yet:

   $$
   \begin{aligned}
   v_{\mathrm{esc}} &= \left(\frac{2GM_{\oplus}}{r_{\oplus}}\right)^{1/2}
     \\[0.8em]
   &= \left(\frac{2\left(6.674 \times 10^{-8}\
        \mathrm{cm^{3}\,g^{-1}\,s^{-2}}\right)
        \left(5.97 \times 10^{27}\ \mathrm{g}\right)}
        {6.37 \times 10^{8}\ \mathrm{cm}}\right)^{1/2}
   \end{aligned}
   $$

   **Now cancel the units, still without touching the numbers.** On top,
   $\mathrm{cm^{3}\,g^{-1}\,s^{-2}} \times \mathrm{g} =
   \mathrm{cm^{3}\,s^{-2}}$. Dividing that by the $\mathrm{cm}$ underneath
   leaves $\mathrm{cm^{2}\,s^{-2}}$, and the square root of that is

   $$
   \left(\mathrm{cm^{2}\,s^{-2}}\right)^{1/2} = \mathrm{cm\,s^{-1}}.
   $$

   *Do the units make sense?* A speed is a length over a time, so yes. **This
   is the step that catches mistakes early.** Had you forgotten to take the
   square root, the answer would have come out in $\mathrm{cm^{2}\,s^{-2}}$ —
   which is not a speed, and you would know something was wrong before doing a
   single multiplication.

   **Only now, the numbers.**

   $$
   v_{\mathrm{esc}} = \left(\frac{7.97 \times 10^{20}}
                                 {6.37 \times 10^{8}}\right)^{1/2}
     \mathrm{cm\,s^{-1}}
   = \left(1.25 \times 10^{12}\right)^{1/2}\ \mathrm{cm\,s^{-1}}
   = 1.12 \times 10^{6}\ \mathrm{cm\,s^{-1}}
   $$

   Centimeters per second is not how anyone quotes a speed like this, so
   convert, with the equivalence written as a fraction so the centimeters
   cancel:

   $$
   v_{\mathrm{esc}} = 1.12 \times 10^{6}\ \mathrm{cm\,s^{-1}} \times
     \frac{1\ \mathrm{km}}{10^{5}\ \mathrm{cm}}
   = 11\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}
   $$

   About eleven kilometers every second — and that is why getting off this
   planet is hard.
   :::

2. How far from the center of the Earth do we need to be for the escape velocity
   to be a modest highway speed of $100\ \mathrm{km\ hr^{-1}}$?

   ::: {.callout-note .help-answer collapse="true" title="Answer"}
   The distance works out to $1.03 \times 10^{14}\ \mathrm{cm}$, which is
   $1.03 \times 10^{9}\ \mathrm{km}$, or about $6.9\,\mathrm{AU}$ — roughly
   Saturn's distance from the Sun, and some $160{,}000$ Earth radii out.
   :::

:::

## The Schwarzschild radius

The Schwarzschild radius is a key concept for black holes.  We'll talk
more about it next time, but is, in some ways, the "size" of a black
hole.  We'll be more precise later.  For now, let's see how to
calculate it.

::: {.panel-tabset .tracks}

### Physical intuition

We can imagine taking an object of a given mass $M$ and shrinking its radius $r$
until escape velocity at that radius is the speed of light. Then, because that's
Nature's speed limit, we have something too massive to escape!

### Mathematical explanation

Take @eq-vesc and set the escape velocity equal to the speed of light:

$$
v_{\mathrm{esc}} = \left(\frac{2 G M}{r}\right)^{1/2} = c
$$

which leads to

$$
r_S = \frac{2 G M}{c^2}.
$$ {#eq-schwarzschild}

This is called the Schwarzschild radius.

### Numerical exploration

@eq-schwarzschild is a one-line calculation, but the answers span an absurd
range. Here it is evaluated over a ladder of masses, printed in whatever unit
keeps the number readable.

The code uses [astropy](https://www.astropy.org), which carries physical
constants and units as first-class objects: `const.G` and `const.c` know their
own units, and `.to(u.km)` converts. You will see a lot of it in this course.

```{python}
#| label: rs-ladder

from astropy import constants as const
from astropy import units as u


def r_S(M):
    """Schwarzschild radius for a mass M, as a length in cm."""
    return (2 * const.G * M / const.c**2).to(u.cm)


def human_units(r):
    """Convert a length to whichever unit keeps the number readable."""
    if r < 1 * u.km:
        return r.to(u.cm)
    if r < 1 * u.au:
        return r.to(u.km)
    return r.to(u.au)


# Any astropy Quantity works as a mass: 70 * u.kg, 1.4 * u.M_sun, 5.97e27 * u.g
masses = [
    ("Earth",            const.M_earth),
    ("the Sun",          const.M_sun),
    ("10 solar masses",  10 * const.M_sun),
    ("1e6 solar masses", 1e6 * const.M_sun),
    ("1e9 solar masses", 1e9 * const.M_sun),
]

for label, M in masses:
    print(f"{label:>18}   M = {M.to(u.g):10.3e}   r_S = {human_units(r_S(M)):>12.4g}")
```

#| autorun: false

from astropy import constants as const
from astropy import units as u


def r_S(M):
    """Schwarzschild radius for a mass M, as a length in cm."""
    return (2 * const.G * M / const.c**2).to(u.cm)


def human_units(r):
    """Convert a length to whichever unit keeps the number readable."""
    if r < 1 * u.km:
        return r.to(u.cm)
    if r < 1 * u.au:
        return r.to(u.km)
    return r.to(u.au)


# Any astropy Quantity works as a mass: 70 * u.kg, 1.4 * u.M_sun, 5.97e27 * u.g
masses = [                          # <- edit this list
    ("Earth",            const.M_earth),
    ("the Sun",          const.M_sun),
    ("10 solar masses",  10 * const.M_sun),
    ("1e6 solar masses", 1e6 * const.M_sun),
    ("1e9 solar masses", 1e9 * const.M_sun),
]

for label, M in masses:
    print(f"{label:>18}   M = {M.to(u.g):10.3e}   r_S = {human_units(r_S(M)):>12.4g}")
